documents.title: IUGA ICS Joint Report on Terminology for Female Pelvic Floor Dysfunction

chunks.content: Introduction Overactive bladder (OAB) is characterized by urinary urgency with or without incontinence, usually accompanied by increased frequency and nocturia. , , The prevalence of OAB increases with age and it compromises social participation and quality of life. , Data from cross-sectional studies confirm the high prevalence of OAB in diverse populations. Despite its impact, older adults often consider urinary urgency a normal part of ageing and they tend to delay seeking care. , Similarly, functional independence relies on the ability to perform instrumental activities of daily living (IADL), such as shopping, managing medications, and using transportation, and deficits in these tasks predict disability and institutionalization. , Cultural adaptations of the Lawton scale indicates its reliable assessment of functional ability across populations. Hence, maintaining continence and IADL are central to healthy ageing. , Continence is closely linked to several domains of intrinsic capacity, including locomotion, cognition, and psychological well-being. Within the World Health Organization-Integrated Care for Older People (WHO-ICOPE) framework, urinary symptoms can contribute to reduced mobility, social withdrawal, and loss of independence, making continence an important component of maintaining functional ability in older adults. The WHO-ICOPE framework provides evidence-based recommendations to help preserve locomotion, cognition, vitality, psychological well-being, vision, and hearing. , Multidomain programs derived from ICOPE have demonstrated benefits for mobility and nutritional status, but urinary symptoms or IADL have rarely been evaluated. Pelvic floor muscle training is a recommended first-line therapy for OAB and can reduce urgency and incontinence when delivered intensively or combined with pharmacotherapy. , , However, a systematic review noted heterogeneity across trials and concluded that evidence remains inconclusive. Thus, the effects of general multidomain programs that only incorporate brief bladder management components remain unclear. The physiotherapy-led integrated care program (PTICOPE) was designed to enhance the intrinsic capacity of older Malaysians through multidomain interventions. The parent trial evaluated all six main intrinsic capacity domains. Recognizing the burden of OAB and the importance of IADL, exploratory secondary analysis was conducted to examine whether PTICOPE improves OAB symptoms and IADL compared with usual care. In contrast to bladder-specific rehabilitation trials that deliver high-intensity pelvic floor training, in the present study, we evaluated continence outcomes within a real-world, WHO-ICOPE aligned multidomain integrated care program. By examining urinary and functional outcomes in a community-based intrinsic capacity framework, our analysis aimed to provide insights into whether multidomain interventions alone are sufficient to influence bladder-related outcomes or if dedicated bladder-focused strategies remain necessary. This secondary analysis was planned a priori to explore continence-related outcomes not addressed in the primary trial and was specified in the original trial protocol registered with the Thai Clinical Trials Registry (TCTR20241029007). Materials and Methods Study design and participants This exploratory secondary analysis used data from a single-blind, parallel-group randomized controlled trial, which was prospectively registered with the Thai Clinical Trials Registry (TCTR20241029007). Community-dwelling adults aged 60–75 years were recruited in Kedah, Malaysia. The upper age limit was applied to ensure that participants could safely participate in the multidomain exercise components of the intervention and to maintain a relatively homogeneous functional profile among community-dwelling older adults. The inclusion criteria were community-dwelling adults who lived independently in the community, ability to ambulate with or without an assistive device, and provision of written informed consent. Exclusion criteria included severe cognitive impairment, recent urological surgery, or medical conditions that could limit safe participation in exercise, such as unstable cardiac disease, uncontrolled hypertension, or severe musculoskeletal disorders affecting mobility. The protocol was approved by the university's research ethics committee, and written informed consent was obtained. Randomization and masking Participants were randomly assigned at a 1:1 ratio to PTICOPE or usual care using computer-generated sequences with concealed allocation. The trial used a single-blind design where outcome assessors were blinded to group allocation. Participants and physiotherapists who delivered the intervention could not be blinded due to the nature of the program. Interventions PTICOPE comprised four center-based sessions (weeks 1, 4, 8, and 12) led by physiotherapists. Each session of 60–75 min addressed locomotion, cognition, vitality, psychological well-being, vision, and hearing according to ICOPE guidance. A brief pelvic floor and bladder management component was included, where participants were taught pelvic floor exercises and bladder retraining strategies and received advice on fluid intake and voiding routines. Home-based exercises were prescribed, and adherence was encouraged through weekly telephone or WhatsApp contacts. Usual care participants attended four visits during which they received general health education, and structured exercises or continence training were not provided. Detailed descriptions of the PTICOPE intervention components and the TIDieR reporting checklist are provided in Supplementary Appendix S1. Outcomes OAB symptoms were assessed at baseline (week 1) and post-intervention (week 12) using the eight-item Malay OAB Questionnaire-V8 (OAB-V8). Detailed descriptions of the PTICOPE intervention components and the TIDieR reporting checklist are provided in Supplementary Appendix S1. Outcomes OAB symptoms were assessed at baseline (week 1) and post-intervention (week 12) using the eight-item Malay OAB Questionnaire-V8 (OAB-V8). This instrument evaluates urinary urgency, frequency, nocturia, urge incontinence, and the degree of symptom bother. Each item is scored from 0 (not at all) to 5 (a very great deal), yielding a total score range of 0–40, where higher scores indicate greater symptom severity and a score ≥8 is commonly used as a screening threshold suggestive of OAB. It has been demonstrated that the Malay version of OAB-V8 has good internal consistency and construct validity in Malaysian populations (Cronbach's α ≈ 0.80). IADL ratings were measured using the Malay Activities of Daily Living Questionnaire (ADLQ), which assesses eight domains comprising telephone use, shopping, food preparation, housekeeping, laundry, transportation, medication management, and financial handling. Scores range from 0 (dependent) to 8 (independent). The Malay version of the ADLQ has shown good validity and reliability, with reported internal consistency coefficients exceeding 0.80. , The OAB-V8 is primarily designed as a screening instrument for identifying symptoms of OAB rather than as a tool for monitoring treatment responses; thus, its ability to detect small changes in symptom severity over time may be limited. Data collection procedures Data were collected prospectively as part of the parent single-blind randomized controlled trial. Screening and baseline assessments were conducted prior to randomization at participating Pusat Aktiviti Warga Emas (PAWE) community centers in the Kulim, Sungai Petani, and Yan districts. Centers were selected based on the number of registered participants and the local prevalence of older adults aged 60–75 years, as reported by the Department of Statistics Malaysia. Follow-up assessments were performed in the same centers at week 12. Outcome data were collected by trained assessors who were independent of intervention delivery. Standardized assessment procedures were applied across all study sites to ensure consistent data collection. Validated Malay language instruments were administered in a face-to-face manner. Participants completed OAB-V8 and IADL assessments at baseline and week 12. No additional measurements were obtained for this secondary analysis, and only data collected prospectively during the parent trial were included in the present analyses. Statistical analysis The sample size in the parent trial (n = 70) was calculated to detect changes in intrinsic capacity outcomes rather than urinary or functional outcomes. Therefore, no separate sample size calculation was performed for OAB-V8 or IADL in this secondary analysis. With the available sample size, the study was probably only able to detect moderate-to-large intervention effects, whereas smaller but potentially clinically relevant differences may have remained undetected. Participants with complete baseline and week 12 data were analyzed (complete-case approach). Baseline characteristics were compared using t -tests or χ 2 tests. Within-group changes were examined using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests due to non-normality. Between-group differences at week 12 were detected using analysis of covariance, adjusting for baseline score and age, and partial η 2 indicated the effect size. The baseline score was included to account for baseline differences between groups and to improve statistical precision, and age was included because a statistically significant baseline imbalance was observed between groups. Statistically significant differences were accepted at p < 0.05. However, given the exploratory nature of this secondary analysis and the limited sample size, this study was probably only powered to detect moderate-to-large effects. Therefore, smaller but potentially clinically meaningful differences may not have been detected. Results Flow of participants Seventy individuals were randomized (35 per group). Seven withdrew before the assessment in week 12 (four intervention, three control) due to relocation or personal reasons. The remaining 63 participants (32 intervention, 31 control) had complete baseline and week-12 OAB and IADL data, and were included in the secondary analysis ( ). Baseline characteristics The mean age of the participants was 66.8 ± 4.5 years, and they were predominantly female (73%). The intervention group members were slightly older (68.25 ± 4.39 vs 65.35 ± 4.17 years, p = 0.009) and had higher baseline IADL scores (7.41 ± 0.61 vs 6.90 ± 0.70, p = 0.004); therefore, age and baseline outcome scores were included as covariates in the adjusted analyses. Other characteristics were similar, including OAB-V8 scores (11.69 ± 5.67 vs 10.45 ± 4.40) and comorbidities ( ). At baseline, the mean OAB-V8 scores in both groups were close to the lower end of the scale, indicating mild urinary symptoms, whereas their IADL scores were near the upper limit, reflecting a high level of functional independence in IADL. Other characteristics were similar, including OAB-V8 scores (11.69 ± 5.67 vs 10.45 ± 4.40) and comorbidities ( ). At baseline, the mean OAB-V8 scores in both groups were close to the lower end of the scale, indicating mild urinary symptoms, whereas their IADL scores were near the upper limit, reflecting a high level of functional independence in IADL. This limited scope for measurable improvement may have contributed to the absence of significant between-group differences at follow-up. OAB and IADL outcomes In the intervention group, median OAB-V8 scores increased slightly from 10.0 (interquartile range (IQR) = 8.0–13.0) at baseline to 12.0 (IQR = 9.0–14.5) at 12 weeks, although this change was not statistically significant (Z = −1.95, p = 0.051). No significant within-group change was observed in the control group ( ). The median IADL scores remained stable within both groups. After adjustment for baseline scores and age, no significant between-group differences were observed at week 12 for OAB-V8 (adjusted mean = 11.22 ± 0.25 vs 11.76 ± 0.25; F (1,60) = 2.27, p = 0.137, partial η 2 = 0.036) or IADL (adjusted mean = 7.17 ± 0.08 vs 7.08 ± 0.08; F (1,60) = 0.73, p = 0.398, partial η 2 = 0.012) ( ). Minor musculoskeletal soreness occurred in 12% of participants and resolved spontaneously, and no serious adverse events were reported. summarizes the within-group changes in the OAB-V8 and IADL scores over 12 weeks. The median line graphs indicated a slight increase in the OAB-V8 scores for the intervention group (10–12), whereas the scores remained unchanged in the control group, indicating no improvement in OAB symptoms. The median IADL scores remained stable in both groups (7–7), with complete overlap of intervention and control lines, reflecting a ceiling effect and stability of IADL performance ( ). These visual trends were consistent with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test results, which demonstrated no significant within-group changes in either outcome. After adjustment for baseline values and age, the adjusted mean OAB-V8 and IADL scores at 12 weeks did not differ significantly between the intervention and control groups, indicating no detectable intervention effect on either outcome. Discussion In this exploratory secondary analysis, we found no significant effect of a multidomain integrated care program on OAB symptoms or IADL scores over 12 weeks. Between-group differences were small and within-group changes minimal, indicating that PTICOPE did not lead to measurable improvements in continence or IADL compared with usual care within the study period. The reported effect sizes were small (partial η 2 = 0.036 for OAB-V8 and 0.012 for IADL), indicating that the magnitude of the observed group differences was minimal and unlikely to represent clinically meaningful improvement during the 12-week intervention period. This study enhanced our knowledge by evaluating bladder and IADL outcomes within a physiotherapy-led multidomain integrated care model aligned with the WHO-ICOPE framework. Previous multidomain intervention studies focused primarily on mobility, nutrition, or intrinsic capacity domains, whereas few explicitly assessed urinary symptoms. Conversely, pelvic floor rehabilitation trials have demonstrated efficacy under structured, high-intensity protocols. The present analysis bridged these fields by examining whether a general multidomain program incorporating only a brief bladder component could meaningfully influence urinary and IADL outcomes in community-dwelling older adults. The minimal increase in OAB-V8 scores for the intervention group should be interpreted cautiously. The median score change was small and no significant difference was observed between the groups after adjustment, suggesting that the pattern may reflect normal variation in symptom reporting. Increased awareness of urinary symptoms following education regarding pelvic floor exercises and bladder habits may also have influenced the responses, and the OAB-V8 is primarily a screening tool, so small changes in score might not indicate clinically meaningful deterioration. The lack of significant improvements in the OAB-V8 and IADL scores should also be interpreted in light of the participants’ baseline status. The median baseline OAB-V8 scores were only slightly above the screening threshold (≥8), indicating generally mild urinary symptoms, whereas the baseline IADL scores were close to the upper limit of the scale, reflecting high baseline IADL scores. The proportions of male and female participants were comparable in the groups at baseline. However, differences related to sex in terms of urinary symptoms or functional performance may still have influenced the outcomes and cannot be excluded completely. It should also be noted that the participants in both groups had relatively high IADL scores at baseline, and thus there was little capacity for measurable improvement over the course of the intervention. It should also be noted that the participants in both groups had relatively high IADL scores at baseline, and thus there was little capacity for measurable improvement over the course of the intervention. The bladder management component of PTICOPE was brief and delivered infrequently. Effective continence interventions typically require high-intensity pelvic floor muscle training and structured behavioral retraining. A randomized trial combining intensive pelvic floor training with solifenacin obtained greater improvements in OAB symptoms than medication alone, supporting the importance of the intervention's specificity and dose. Conversely, a systematic review reported that evidence for pelvic floor muscle training remains inconclusive due to heterogeneity and small sample sizes. Thus, the low-dose behavioral component within PTICOPE was unlikely to have produced meaningful changes in urinary symptoms. The characteristics of the outcome measure may also have influenced the results. In this study, OAB symptoms were assessed using the OAB-V8, which is primarily intended for identifying individuals with possible OAB rather than monitoring the response to treatment. Consequently, small changes in symptoms during the intervention period may not have been fully captured. Future investigations could consider using more detailed assessment approaches, such as bladder diaries or validated patient-reported instruments like the OAB Questionnaire (OAB-q), which could more comprehensively evaluate the frequency of symptoms and their impacts on daily functioning. Similarly, the high baseline IADL scores limited the potential for observing functional gains. In addition, this secondary analysis was underpowered for OAB and IADL outcomes, and modest intervention effects cannot be excluded. Given the relatively small sample size for participants with complete outcome data, our study probably only had sufficient statistical power to detect moderate to large intervention effects. Therefore, smaller but clinically relevant improvements in OAB symptoms or IADL may have remained undetected. Consequently, the absence of statistically significant findings should be interpreted cautiously and treated as exploratory observations that require confirmation in adequately powered trials. These findings are consistent with reports indicating that general multidomain interventions improved mobility and overall well-being but their impacts on continence were limited when bladder management was not a primary focus. , By contrast, bladder-specific programs that incorporated pelvic floor training, bladder retraining, or neuromodulation resulted in larger reductions in urgency and incontinence. , , Improvements in IADL are more likely among individuals with baseline impairment and when task-specific training is delivered over longer durations. , Strengths and limitations The strengths of this study include its randomized design, allocation concealment, blinded outcome assessment, and adherence to CONSORT guidelines for secondary analyses. The limitations of this study include its exploratory nature and small sample size, incomplete blinding of participants, low intensity of the pelvic floor component, and the use of OAB-V8, which is primarily a screening tool and may be less sensitive for detecting small changes over time. In addition, the study population was limited to adults aged 60–75 years, which may reduce the generalizability of the results to older populations, particularly those aged ≥80 years who often experience greater functional decline and urinary symptoms. Thus, the generalizability of our findings is limited to relatively healthy, community-dwelling older adults. Implications Integrated care programs may support the intrinsic capacity and stability of IADL performance but are unlikely to improve continence or IADL without dedicated, high-dose bladder-focused strategies. Future trials should recruit participants with clinically significant OAB or functional limitations, deliver targeted pelvic floor and bladder training alongside multidomain elements, use sensitive outcome measures, and ensure adequate power and follow-up durations. Our findings inform clinicians that multidomain community programs may preserve IADL performance but targeted bladder interventions should be incorporated when continence outcomes are prioritized. Conclusion According to this exploratory secondary analysis, PTICOPE did not significantly improve OAB symptoms or IADL compared with usual care over 12 weeks. Outcomes remained stable in both groups, suggesting that the multidomain intervention maintained but did not substantially modify bladder-related or functional outcomes. These findings indicate that WHO-ICOPE aligned multidomain programs may help to preserve the functional status but are unlikely to improve continence when bladder management is not a primary component. Therefore, targeted, adequately dosed bladder-focused interventions may be necessary when reduced urinary symptoms are a primary therapeutic goal. Ethical approval This study adhered to the ethical standards of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Universiti Teknologi MARA Research Ethics Committee (REC/09/2024 [PG/MR/437]). The approval remains valid until November 2026. The trial was registered with the Thai Clinical Trials Registry (TCTR20241029007). All participants provided written informed consent.
